summary: After a city's minimum wage rose a second time, low-wage workers earned a higher rate but worked fewer hours, so the paycheck stayed flat, in a study others contest.
realLife: A University of Washington study for Seattle's council used state quarterly hours and earnings data. After the minimum reached the higher step, hourly pay in low-wage jobs rose by roughly three percent but hours fell by about as much, so earnings stayed flat against comparable cities; the study found the raise hurt low-wage workers on balance, and the finding is contested. The first smaller step showed little change. Some owners said they hired for fewer shifts and one also cut some employees' hours, while a student working full time said the raise helped him save for school.
sources: https://kuow.org/stories/minimum-wage-increase-hurt-seattles-low-wage-workers-study-says (KUOW news story on the UW study of Seattle's wage rise: hours down about as much as pay rose)

turns.pulledBy: an employer with thin margins and a large step
